Chuck Lorre Dishes On His New Memoir ‘Sitcom’ Image Credit: Sonja Flemming/CBS Chuck Lorre is making the rounds to promote Sitcom , his memoir about hatching and EP-ing some of the biggest sitcom successes. The Long Island-born wannabe musician fell into the comedy game and was involved in the creation of The Big Bang Theory , Two and a Half Men , Young Sheldon , Bookie, Dharma & Greg, Mike & Molly, Mom and others. Lorre’s book includes those vanity cards after the closing credits, plus marked-up pilot scripts from Two and a Half Men, The Kominsky Method and The Big Bang Theory . While helping to create stars of the likes of Jim Parsons, Melissa McCarthy, Allison Janney and others who handled sudden fame and riches well, much of the memoir’s propulsive narrative focuses on the difficult stars who used sudden fame to become narcissistic and make life unnecessarily hard for those around them. Read the full interview here.

‘La Bola Negra’ Directors Javier Ambrossi & Javier Calvo Reveal The Secrets Of Their Spanish Epic Image Credit: Getty Images Penélope Cruz had been a muse to Los Javis — the moniker for Spanish filmmakers Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo — for years before they met for lunch to persuade her to play a singer (more a force of nature, really) in La Bola Negra , an electrifying sensation at Cannes that’s now Spain’s entry for best international feature film Oscar . “I saw her in a clip of Jamón Jamón ,” says Ambrossi, referring to Bigas Luna’s 1992 picture, in which Cruz appeared for the first time opposite her now-husband Javier Bardem. “I was young, and I thought, ‘Who is she ?!’” Calvo was similarly enchanted when he saw Cruz in Pedro Almodóvar’s 1999 Oscar winner All About My Mother . “She’s got that material of the stars,” he says. “When you put a camera in front of her, she can do anything, and she doesn’t even realize what she’s doing. There’s a power , there’s a force guiding her, and that’s amazing to see first-hand.” Read the interview with Los Javis here.

How Alec Baldwin Reacted To Rory Kennedy’s New Doc About His ‘Rust’ Trial Image Credit: Ramsay de Give-Pool/Getty Images Mystery still surrounds the fatal shooting on the set of Alec Baldwin ’s Western Rust , an incident that claimed the life of cinematographer Halyna Hutchins. Did the actor pull the trigger on a prop gun as he rehearsed a scene (he denies that), or did the weapon malfunction and misfire? How did a live round get into the revolver and who brought the lethal ammunition to the set? Why were prosecutors in Santa Fe, NM so intent on charging Baldwin with a crime for what many impartial observers — though not all — saw as a tragic accident? The answers to some of those questions are provided in the new documentary The Trial of Alec Baldwin , directed by Rory Kennedy , which opens in Los Angeles on Friday. The film begins by dispelling one false rumor – that Baldwin initiated the project as some sort of attempt to repair his damaged reputation. Text on screen states flatly, “Baldwin was given no editorial control, nor did he provide any financial support or receive any compensation.” Read the full story here.

Ron Perlman’s New Hemingway Biopic Image Credit: Jack Guy Ron Perlman is still a man of action. The indefatigable Hellboy and Sons of Anarchy star, now 76, has half a dozen films in production, and next year is aiming to play Ernest Hemingway in a new biopic set in Cuba and will co-star in the anticipated Sons of Anarchy spinoff Legends . A year on from Deadline announcing the launch of Perlman’s Asylm Studios banner , we caught up with the veteran actor (who made his screen debut almost 50 years ago) and the company’s co-founder Willie Morris about their indie slate and Perlman’s anticipated studio projects. Read the full interview here.

The ‘Street Fighter’ Review Taking a cue from various attempts to breathe cinematic life into the Mortal Kombat franchise, including one earlier this year, another oldie but goodie from the heyday and beloved universe of video game classics is taking a swing at appealing to new generations of fans who weren’t even born when the iconic game Street Fighter first appeared in 1987. In addition to various animated and TV series takes, there have been a couple of big-screen attempts, the most notable in 1994 with Jean-Claude Van Damme’s Street Fighter which was a box office hit. However, the 2009 attempt, Street Fighter: The Legend Of Chun-Li, was a miserable flop. Now with Legendary and the game’s creator Capcom teaming up we have a new and perhaps the most elaborate reboot yet. Whether anyone was asking for it is another question. Read the review here.

EXCLUSIVE: United Artists isn’t done adding to an already loaded film slate as sources tell Deadline that Scott Stuber’s company and Amazon MGM Studios have greenlit an untitled thriller with Denzel Washington set to star Christopher McQuarrie on board to direct. Scott Barkan and Gregg Zehentner penned the script.

The film will bow in theaters on October 1, 2027.

The plot centers on a former police detective serving a life sentence who is diagnosed with terminal brain cancer. Granted compassionate release with six months to live, he returns home to the estranged daughter he left behind and a grandson he never knew existed. He only wants to make amends and forget his dark past, but his dark past has not forgotten him.

Related Stories

Andrew Dice Clay Latest To Join Benny Safdie's 'Lizard Music'

United Artists, Amazon MGM & Steven Spielberg's 'Mandela Catalogue' Sets Summer 2028 Release

McQuarrie will also produce alongside Heather McQuarrie along with Stuber and Nick Nesbitt, who produce through United Artists; Joseph Restaino for Hungry Bull Productions; Reza Moheet and Norman Aladjem for Mainstay Entertainment; Katia Washington; and Tommy Harper. Hungry Bull’s Tony Stopperan, Mainstay’s Tim Honigman and Joe Guest will serve as executive producers

Watch on Deadline

As for Washington, the two-time Oscar winner had been planning to reunite with Antoine Fuqua this fall for the Netflix epic about ancient Carthaginian general Hannibal. Those plans were put on pause when pre-production was halted following budgetary issues. The stoppage allowed Washington to refocus on other projects, with this film moving to the top of the list following meetings with McQuarrie that ultimately led to Washington giving the thumbs-up. Producers will now look to fill the role of Washington’s daughter.

Most recently, Washington has made his return to the Broadway stage in Othello alongside Jake Gyllenhaal, and starred in Spike Lee’s Highest 2 Lowest . Up next, he will star in Netflix’s The Take (formerly titled Here Comes the Flood ) alongside Robert Pattinson and Daisy Edgar-Jones. That film is slated to release in 2027.

After a decade redefining the modern action spectacle with Mission: Impossible , Oscar winner McQuarrie returns to the crime genre he helped define with films like Jack Reacher , The Way of the Gun and The Usual Suspects . He most recently helped helm the last four Mission: Impossible films including the most recent Mission: Impossible -The Final Reckoning.

With UA, Stuber is now in production on Lizard Music , the next collaboration between Dwayne Johnson and Benny Safdie. It is also in post-production on a new version of Highlander starring Henry Cavill, and is prepping Michael Mann’s Heat 2 starring Leonardo DiCaprio and Christian Bale, and The Mandela Catalogue , the analog horror adaptation with Steven Spielberg’s Amblin Entertainment to be directed by series creator Alex Kister.

In partnership with Ben Affleck and Matt Damon’s Artist Equity Independent Pictures, Hungry Bull recently wrapped production on Downriver starring Jessica Biel, Garrett Hedlund and Jake Lacy.

Next up for Mainstay on the big screen is the genre-bending vampire western The Sun Always Sets in the West at Lionsgate, set for a 2027 start date. On TV, Mainstay recently produced The Matchmaker with Patti Stanger at the CW.

Washington is represented by WME. McQuarrie is represented by CAA and Greenberg Glusker. Barkan and Zehentner are represented by Mainstay Entertainment and Hansen, Jacobson, Teller, Hoberman, Newman, Warren, Richman, Rush, Kaller, Gellman, Meigs & Fox.

editorial_title_zh: CEWE Photo Award：来自瑞士的月度获奖者马蒂亚斯·布克哈特（Matthias Burkhard）
editorial_excerpt_zh: 在CEWE国际摄影大赛中，来自世界各地的摄影爱好者可以提交作品，参赛时间长达一年。此外，评委们每个月还会评选出四幅照片。在当前的比赛中，来自瑞士的马蒂亚斯·布克哈特（Matthias Burkhard）成为了月度获奖者并接受了采访……
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "由在21个国家开展业务的CEWE摄影冲印实验室主办的“CEWE Photo Award”是全球最大的国际摄影大赛之一。当前的2027年赛事于2026年5月启动。自那时起，业余摄影爱好者和专业摄影师均可在2027年5月底之前，以“我们的世界真美丽”（Our world is "https://www.fotointern.ch/archiv/2026/06/05/cewe-photo-award-2027-ab-sofort-foto-einreichen/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "月度获奖者：此外，每个月还会从所有类别中评选出三幅照片，以及从“青年才俊奖”（Young Photo Awards", "url": "https://contest.cewe.de/cewephotoaward2027/de_ch/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "对CEWE Photo Award瑞士月度获奖者马蒂亚斯·布克哈特（Matthias Burkhard）的采访", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在群山、阿尔卑斯山转场与日出之间：一位来自内阿彭策尔的业余摄影师讲述他的摄影狂热", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "CEWE Photo Award 收到了来自世界各地的众多摄影作品。内阿彭策尔的马蒂亚斯·布克哈特（Matthias Burkhard）也将他最好的照片提交到了比赛中。结果非常成功：他拍摄于“旅行与文化”（Travel & Culture）类别的照片《阿尔卑斯山转场中的盖斯布布》（Gaisbub beim Öberefahre）入选了2027年6月的四幅最佳国际照片。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.fotointern.ch/wp-uploads/2026/10/CEWE-Photo-Award-2027-Monatsgewinner-CH-Matthias-Burkhard-8.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Fotointern", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "马蒂亚斯·布克哈特（Matthias Burkhard）的月度获奖作品《阿尔卑斯山转场中的盖斯布布》（Gaisbub beim Öberefahre）", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "亲爱的马蒂亚斯，祝贺你取得这一伟大的成就！我们很高兴能认识你。请跟我们简单聊聊你自己以及你对摄影的热情。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我叫马蒂亚斯·布克哈特（Matthias Burkhard），在美丽的阿彭策尔地区出生并长大。如今我和妻子以及儿子一起住在博登湖畔阿尔特瑙（Altnau）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在闲暇之余，我全身心地投入到摄影中。这一切始于2017年的一趟缅甸之旅，当时我专门为此买了一台相机。我拍的一些早期照片出奇地成功，这激发了我对摄影的热情。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "经历了一次运动受伤后，我无法再从事当时的那项爱好，于是开始经常徒步旅行，探索阿尔卑斯山脉（Alpstein）的山峦——当然，背包里总是装着相机。就这样，徒步与摄影结合在了一起。通过每一次出行和每一张照片，我都学到了一些新东西。哪怕某张照片没拍好，我也坚持了下来，并试图在下一次做得更好。我最喜欢在黄金时刻或蓝色时刻、围绕日出和日落时分拍摄风景。野生动物以及近来迷上的微距摄影也让我深深着迷。此外，家庭照片对我也非常重要，因为它们能定格美好的回忆。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你荣获 CEWE Photo Award 的作品《阿尔卑斯山转场中的盖斯布布》（Gaisbub beim Öberefahre）是如何诞生的？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这幅获奖照片是6月初在阿彭策尔地区的一次阿尔卑斯山转场（Alpaufzug）期间拍摄的。今年，我非常想亲身体验并拍摄这一过程。为此我不得不很早起床。我想当时大概是凌晨两三点。由于奶牛在转场期间会封锁道路，我必须及时赶到现场。因此我在黑暗中就出发了，随后在那里等待了几个小时。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在那段时间里，我得以享受山中的宁静与氛围，当然也拍了其他一些照片。不知何时，我听到远处传来的牛铃声，心里知道：要开始了。我找了一个稍微远离其他观众的位置，等待着正确的时机。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "照片中的那个男孩走在阿尔卑斯山转场的最前面。他是最早迎面走向我的人之一，也是我拍摄的首批拍摄对象之一。他看起来无比自豪，能走在队伍最前面。这个场景瞬间打动了我。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你当时就立刻知道这是一张与众不同的照片吗？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我在现场就注意到自己非常喜欢这个场景。我通常在拍摄后立刻检查我的照片，看看清晰度和曝光是否合适。但照片是否真的有特别之处，往往要等到事后在电脑前才能看出来。不过对于这张照片，我很快就知道它可能会是一张不错的作品。这个男孩有着惊人的感染力，显得十分骄傲。与此同时，这张照片也展现了阿彭策尔传统的重要部分：传统牧民盛装（Sennentracht）、牲畜以及阿尔卑斯山转场时的清晨氛围。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这张照片对你意味着什么？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对我而言，这张照片的意义远比第一眼看上去要丰富得多。我给它取名为《盖斯布布》（Gaisbub）。旁观者看到的可能只是一个身穿传统服饰的男孩、牲畜和一片美丽的草地。但对我来说，整个故事都与这张照片紧密相连。当我看着它时，我的思绪瞬间回到了那个地方。我听到了铃声，想起了牧民们的约德尔唱法（Jodeln），以及阿尔卑斯山转场期间弥漫的氛围。我还记得自己当时是怎么站在那里的，等了多久，以及对于关键时刻能否成功拍下感到多么紧张。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "照片带给我的不仅是视觉记忆。有时候，我还会回想起声音、气味或当时的天气。对我而言，一幅影像总是讲述着一个故事，而这个故事往往远远超越了按下快门的那一瞬间。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你为什么偏偏提交了这张照片？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我提交了这次上山赶牛活动的好几张照片。当我浏览时，这张照片立刻吸引了我的眼球。我想：这是一个美好的场景，展现了非常具有阿彭策尔特色的东西。对农民来说，上山赶牛是一年中的高潮。与岁末迎新活动（Silvesterklausen）一起，它属于阿彭策尔地区最重要的传统。因此，我也希望通过这张照片展现一段活生生的民俗。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你很喜欢在瑞士拍照。你对此最看重什么？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我在瑞士最喜欢的拍摄对象显然是山。我特别赞赏瑞士的一点是，它在狭小的空间内呈现出极其丰富的多样性。这里有湖泊、高山湖泊、河流、冰川以及截然不同的风景。野生动物也让我着迷。比如在山区可以观察到羱羊，有时甚至能离它们非常近。从摄影的角度来看，瑞士提供了令人难以置信的丰富内容。即使我多次去同一个地方，每次的氛围也各不相同。光线、天气和季节总是让风景发生变化。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.fotointern.ch/wp-uploads/2026/09/CEWE-Photo-Award-2027-Monatsgewinner-CH-Matthias-Burkhard-3.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Fotointern", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "还有什么你特别想在瑞士拍摄的景致吗？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "几周前我从愿望清单上划掉了一个拍摄对象：阿莱奇冰川。我还有两三个想实现的构想，主要集中在冰川和山脉领域。不过我并没有一张很长的待办清单。许多生活在瑞士的动物，我已经有幸拍过了。如今我也很乐意接受惊喜，到现场看看能拍到什么。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.fotointern.ch/wp-uploads/2026/09/CEWE-Photo-Award-2027-Monatsgewinner-CH-Matthias-Burkhard-7.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Fotointern", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在摄影过程中，有没有哪个瞬间让你经历过并且一直愿意回想起来？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "最难忘的瞬间之一就发生在我的摄影之旅刚开始时，在缅甸。我们在日出时分来到了蒲甘，那是一片巨大的寺庙群。我们骑着踏板车来到一座佛塔并爬了上去。随后，第一缕温暖的光线洒在寺庙上。除此之外，周围还飘浮着附近房屋做饭时产生的炊烟。整个场景宛如魔法。这段经历无疑增强了我对摄影的热情。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.fotointern.ch/wp-uploads/2026/09/CEWE-Photo-Award-2027-Monatsgewinner-CH-Matthias-Burkhard-4.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Fotointern", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "去坦桑尼亚的旅行也给我留下了特别深刻的印象。在一次游猎中，我得以在自然环境中观察并拍摄许多动物。印象最深的是一只猎豹，它在与土狼遭遇后跑进稀树草原，最后爬上了一座小山丘。当时正好是日出，猎豹站在山丘顶上俯瞰着风景。我可以拍无数的照片，但最重要的是，这是一个我可以亲历的无比美妙的时刻。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "另一个亮点是去冰岛的旅行。在一个瀑布，人们可以顺着水流后面走。起初，光影氛围相当平淡无奇。但在日落前不久，太阳出来了，将整个洞穴浸润在温暖的金光中。短短几分钟内，一切都在发光——岩石、水流和洞穴。那真的是一个神奇的时刻，就像太阳快要落山、天空慢慢变成壮丽色彩组合的那一瞬间一样。今天当我看着这张照片时，我在精神上又回到了那里，甚至还能感觉到水珠溅在脸上。", "links": [{"text": "", "url": "https://www.fotointern.ch/wp-uploads/2026/09/CEWE-Photo-Award-2027-Monatsgewinner-CH-Matthias-Burkhard-1.jpg"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.fotointern.ch/wp-uploads/2026/09/CEWE-Photo-Award-2027-Monatsgewinner-CH-Matthias-Burkhard-1.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Fotointern", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "摄影在你的生活中占据什么地位？k", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对我的日常生活来说，摄影是一个创造性的平衡。当我带着相机外出时，我会忘记压力，全神贯注于那一刻。我经常独自出行，因为并不是每个人都有耐心等待特定的光影氛围好几个小时。现在我会先坐下来，观察周围环境，让这个地方对我产生影响。我倾听鸟叫，看着光线如何变化。过去我更专注于立刻拍出一张完美的照片。现在我首先享受当下。摄影帮助我有意识地去感知并更仔细地观察。对我而言，它将技术、创造力和对合适时机的敏锐感觉结合在了一起。", Der von dem in 21 Ländern tätigen CEWE-Fotolabor durchgeführte «CEWE Photo Award» ist einer der grössten internationalen Fotowettbewerbe. Die aktuelle 2027er Ausgabe ist im Mai 2026 gestartet. Seither können Fotoamateure und auch Profis zig Fotos unter dem Motto «Our world is beautiful» in 10 Kategorien bis Ende Mai 2027 einreichen ( Fotointern berichtete ). Insgesamt werden 1000 Fotos mit Preisen im Gesamtwert von über 250’000.- Euro prämiert.

Monatsgewinner : Zusätzlich werden jeden Monat drei Fotos aus allen Kategorien sowie ein Foto aus dem Young Talent Award ausgezeichnet. Die insgesamt vier Gewinner des Monats erhalten jeweils einen CEWE‑Gutschein im Wert von 100 Euro für Fotoprodukte. Alle Monatsgewinner qualifizieren sich automatisch für die Finalauswahl.

Interview mit Matthias Burkhard – Monatsgewinner aus der Schweiz beim CEWE Photo Award

Zwischen Bergen, Alpaufzügen und Sonnenaufgängen Ein Appenzeller Hobbyfotograf erzählt von seiner grossen Leidenschaft

Zahlreiche Fotos aus aller Welt werden beim CEWE Photo Award eingereicht. Auch der Appenzeller Matthias Burkhard hat seine besten Fotos in den Wettbewerb geschickt. Mit Erfolg: Sein Foto «Gaisbub beim Öberefahre» aus der Kategorie Travel & Culture wurde zu einem der vier besten internationalen Fotos im Monat Juni 2027.

Monatsgeweinnerbild «Gaisbub beim Öberefahre» von Matthias Burkhard

Lieber Matthias, herzlichen Glückwunsch zu diesem grossartigen Erfolg! Wir freuen uns, dich kennenzulernen. Erzähl uns gern kurz etwas über dich und deine Leidenschaft für die Fotografie.

Mein Name ist Matthias Burkhard und ich bin im schönen Appenzellerland geboren und aufgewachsen. Heute lebe ich gemeinsam mit meiner Frau und unserem Sohn in Altnau am Bodensee.

In meiner Freizeit widme ich mich leidenschaftlich der Fotografie. Angefangen hat alles im Jahr 2017 während einer Reise nach Myanmar, für die ich mir eigens eine Kamera gekauft hatte. Einige meiner ersten Bilder sind überraschend gut gelungen und so wurde meine Begeisterung für die Fotografie geweckt.

Nach einem Sportunfall konnte ich mein damaliges Hobby nicht mehr ausüben und begann deshalb, regelmässig zu wandern und die Berge des Alpsteins zu erkunden – natürlich immer mit der Kamera im Rucksack. So entstand die Verbindung zwischen Wandern und Fotografieren. Mit jeder Tour und jedem Bild lernte ich etwas dazu. Auch wenn ein Foto nicht gelungen war, blieb ich dran und versuchte, es beim nächsten Mal besser zu machen. Am liebsten fotografiere ich Landschaften während der goldenen oder blauen Stunde, rund um Sonnenauf- und Sonnenuntergänge. Auch die Tierwelt und neuerdings die Makrofotografie faszinieren mich. Besonders wichtig sind mir zudem Familienfotos, da sie schöne Erinnerungen festhalten.

Wie ist dein beim CEWE Photo Award ausgezeichnetes Bild «Gaisbub beim Öberefahre» entstanden?

Das Gewinnerfoto ist Anfang Juni bei einem Alpaufzug im Appenzellerland entstanden. In diesem Jahr wollte ich das Geschehen unbedingt einmal bewusst miterleben und fotografieren. Dafür musste ich sehr früh aufstehen. Ich glaube, es war ungefähr zwei oder drei Uhr morgens. Da die Kühe während des Alpaufzugs die Strassen blockieren, musste ich rechtzeitig vor Ort sein. Ich bin also bereits in der Dunkelheit losgelaufen und habe anschliessend mehrere Stunden gewartet.

In dieser Zeit konnte ich die Ruhe und die Stimmung in den Bergen geniessen und natürlich auch noch andere Fotos aufnehmen. Irgendwann hörte ich in der Ferne die Kuhglocken und wusste: Jetzt geht es los. Ich suchte mir eine Position etwas abseits der anderen Zuschauer und wartete auf den richtigen Moment.

Der Junge auf dem Foto war ganz am Anfang des Alpaufzugs unterwegs. Er war einer der Ersten, die mir entgegenkamen, und auch eines der ersten Motive, die ich fotografiert habe. Er wirkte unglaublich stolz, vorne mitlaufen zu dürfen. Diese Szene hat mich sofort berührt.

Hast du sofort gewusst, dass es ein besonderes Foto werden würde?

Aber ob ein Foto wirklich etwas Besonderes ist, zeigt sich für mich meistens erst später am Computer. Bei diesem Bild wusste ich allerdings schnell, dass es eine schöne Aufnahme sein könnte. Der Junge hatte eine unglaubliche Ausstrahlung und wirkte so stolz. Gleichzeitig zeigt das Foto einen wichtigen Teil der Appenzeller Tradition: die Sennentracht, die Tiere und die morgendliche Stimmung während des Alpaufzugs.

Was bedeutet das Foto für dich?

Für mich bedeutet das Foto viel mehr, als man auf den ersten Blick sieht. Ich habe es «Gaisbub» genannt. Ein Betrachter sieht vielleicht einen Jungen in einer traditionellen Tracht, die Tiere und eine schöne Wiese. Für mich ist aber die ganze Geschichte mit diesem Bild verbunden. Wenn ich es anschaue, bin ich gedanklich sofort wieder dort. Ich höre die Glocken, erinnere mich an das Jodeln der Sennen und an die Stimmung, die während des Alpaufzugs herrschte. Ich weiss noch, wie ich dort stand, wie lange ich gewartet habe und wie nervös ich war, ob der entscheidende Moment gelingen würde.

Fotos lösen bei mir nicht nur visuelle Erinnerungen aus. Manchmal erinnere ich mich auch an Geräusche, Gerüche oder an das Wetter. Ein Bild erzählt für mich immer eine Geschichte und diese Geschichte geht oft weit über den eigentlichen Moment der Aufnahme hinaus.

Warum hast du gerade dieses Foto eingereicht?

Ich habe mehrere Fotos von diesem Alpaufzug eingereicht. Dieses Bild ist mir beim Durchsehen aber sofort ins Auge gesprungen. Ich dachte: Das ist eine schöne Szene und zeigt etwas typisch Appenzellisches. Für die Bauern ist der Alpaufzug ein Höhepunkt des Jahres. Gemeinsam mit dem Silvesterklausen gehört er zu den wichtigsten Traditionen im Appenzellerland. Ich wollte mit dem Foto deshalb auch ein Stück gelebtes Brauchtum zeigen.

Du fotografierst gerne in der Schweiz. Was schätzt du daran besonders?

Meine Lieblingsmotive in der Schweiz sind klar die Berge. Was ich an der Schweiz besonders schätze, ist ihre enorme Vielfalt auf engem Raum. Es gibt Seen, Bergseen, Flüsse, Gletscher und ganz unterschiedliche Landschaften. Auch die Tierwelt fasziniert mich. In den Bergen kann man beispielsweise Steinböcke beobachten und ihnen teilweise erstaunlich nahekommen. Die Schweiz bietet fotografisch unglaublich viel. Selbst wenn ich mehrmals an denselben Ort gehe, ist die Stimmung jedes Mal anders. Das Licht, das Wetter und die Jahreszeit verändern eine Landschaft immer wieder.

Gibt es noch Motive, die du in der Schweiz unbedingt fotografieren möchtest?

Vor einigen Wochen konnte ich ein Motiv von meiner Liste streichen: den Aletschgletscher. Es gibt noch zwei oder drei weitere Ideen, die ich gerne umsetzen möchte vor allem im Bereich der Gletscher und Berge. Eine sehr lange To-do-Liste habe ich aber nicht. Viele Tiere, die in der Schweiz leben, durfte ich bereits fotografieren. Ich lasse mich inzwischen auch gerne überraschen und schaue vor Ort, welche Motive sich ergeben.

Gibt es einen Moment, den du beim Fotografieren erlebt hast und an den du immer wieder gerne zurückdenkst?

Einer der prägendsten Momente war gleich zu Beginn meiner fotografischen Reise in Myanmar. Wir waren bei Sonnenaufgang in Bagan, einer riesigen Tempelanlage. Mit einem Roller fuhren wir zu einer Pagode und stiegen hinauf. Dann fiel das erste warme Licht auf die Tempel. Dazu zogen Rauchschwaden durch die Umgebung, die von den Kochfeuern der umliegenden Häuser stammten. Die ganze Szenerie wirkte magisch. Dieses Erlebnis hat meine Begeisterung für die Fotografie sicher verstärkt.

Auch eine Reise nach Tansania ist mir besonders in Erinnerung geblieben. Auf einer Safari konnte ich viele Tiere in ihrer natürlichen Umgebung beobachten und fotografieren. Besonders eindrücklich war ein Gepard, der nach einer Begegnung mit der Hyäne in die Savanne lief und schliesslich auf einen kleinen Hügel stieg. Es war gerade Sonnenaufgang, und der Gepard stand oben auf dem Hügel und überblickte die Landschaft. Ich konnte unzählige Fotos machen, aber vor allem war es ein unglaublich schöner Moment, den ich miterleben durfte.

Ein weiteres Highlight war eine Reise nach Island. Bei einem Wasserfall konnte man hinter dem Wasser entlanggehen. Zuerst war die Lichtstimmung eher unspektakulär. Doch kurz vor Sonnenuntergang kam die Sonne hervor und tauchte die gesamte Höhle in ein warmes, goldenes Licht. Für ein paar Minuten leuchtete alles gelb – die Felsen, das Wasser und die Höhle. Das war ein wirklich magischer Moment, genauso wie der Augenblick, als die Sonne kurz vor dem Untergang stand und der Himmel sich langsam in ein spektakuläres Farbenspiel verwandelte. Wenn ich das Foto heute anschaue, bin ich gedanklich wieder dort und spüre sogar noch das Wasser in meinem Gesicht.

Welchen Stellenwert hat die Fotografie in deinem Leben?

Die Fotografie ist für mich ein kreativer Ausgleich zu meinem Berufsalltag. Wenn ich mit meiner Kamera unterwegs bin, vergesse ich den Stress und kann mich ganz auf den Moment konzentrieren. Oft bin ich alleine unterwegs, weil nicht jeder die Geduld hat, mehrere Stunden auf eine bestimmte Lichtstimmung zu warten. Ich setze mich heute zuerst hin, beobachte die Umgebung und lasse den Ort auf mich wirken. Ich höre den Vögeln zu und schaue, wie sich das Licht verändert. Früher war ich viel stärker darauf konzentriert, sofort ein perfektes Foto zu machen. Heute geniesse ich zuerst den Moment. Die Fotografie hilft mir, bewusster wahrzunehmen und genauer hinzuschauen. Für mich verbindet sie Technik, Kreativität und das Gespür für den richtigen Augenblick.

Was passiert mit deinen Fotos, nachdem du sie aufgenommen hast?

Meine Fotos sollen nicht einfach auf einer Festplatte verschwinden, sondern möglichst ein zweites Leben bekommen. Deshalb gestalte ich jedes Jahr verschiedene Kalender. Angefangen hat das mit einem CEWE Fotokalender für meine Familie. Mit der Zeit kamen Freunde, Bekannte und Arbeitskollegen dazu, die mittlerweile jedes Jahr einen Kalender bei mir bestellen. Das freut mich besonders, weil es mir zeigt, dass meine Bilder auch anderen Menschen gefallen.

Zusätzlich gestalte ich jedes Jahr einen Tischkalender mit Fotos von meinem Sohn. Einige Fotos hängen zudem in meinem Büro und bei uns zu Hause als Wandbilder. So landen meine Bilder am Ende regelmässig auf Papier und bleiben im Alltag präsent. Kalender gefallen mir besonders, weil die Fotos nicht nur einmal angeschaut werden, sondern mich und andere Menschen über das ganze Jahr begleiten.

Hast du zum Abschluss noch einen Ratschlag für Fotografie-Anfänger?

Man sollte Geduld haben. Fotografie ist ein Lernprozess, den man Schritt für Schritt durchläuft. Am Anfang war ich oft enttäuscht, wenn meine Bilder nicht so aussahen wie die Aufnahmen, die ich auf Instagram gesehen hatte. Meine Fotos waren langweilig oder gaben nicht das wieder, was ich vor Ort erlebt hatte. Mit jeder Tour, jedem Fehler und jedem neuen Bild habe ich aber dazugelernt. Nach und nach beginnt man zu verstehen, wie Licht, Perspektive und Technik zusammenspielen.

Wichtig ist auch, sich nicht nur auf die Kamera zu konzentrieren. Man sollte sich Zeit nehmen, bewusst hinschauen und die Umgebung wahrnehmen. Oft sind es kleine Details, eine besondere Lichtstimmung oder eine ungewohnte Perspektive, die ein Bild interessant machen.

Der wichtigste Tipp ist für mich aber: Fotografiere das, was dich begeistert. Die Technik kann man lernen. Entscheidend ist, dass man Freude an der Fotografie hat und neugierig bleibt. Die besten Bilder entstehen oft dann, wenn man nicht krampfhaft nach dem perfekten Foto sucht.

article_text:
T he buzz surrounding the viral, limb-bending trailer of pre-Halloween horror Other Mommy was such that screen grabs became memes, official YouTube channel views ran up to 30m-plus and BuzzFeed used the extremely BuzzFeed headline : “The Lady Sitting Next To Me SCREAMED”: This Trailer Playing Before The Odyssey Is Scaring Moviegoers, And These Hilarious Reactions Have Me Crying.

Sure, Universal releasing it exclusively attached to the second biggest film of the year played a considerable part but the imagery was efficiently direct and frightening, a derivative scared child/creepy demon set-up turned into something that felt hard to deny and increasingly impossible to avoid. But then what had seemed like the surest slam-dunk horror of the season seemed to slither away. The marketing continued (there was a second trailer that didn’t quite break the internet in the same way) but the reviews never appeared, a choice made to hide the film from critics until the day it opened. It’s a strategic decision that implies a disaster, Universal eager to keep pre-ticket sales high (it’s predicted to win the weekend with $20m-plus) and bad reviews at bay. But instead, as is often the case, it’s less of a one-star train wreck and more of a two-star mess, likely to frustrate rather than enrage.

It’s based on the Bird Box author Josh Malerman’s acclaimed novel Incidents Around the House and the more obvious title change is the clearest indication of what’s shifted from page to screen. Other Mommy is less interested in the slow-burn and more focused on the instant blaze, a rickety fairground ride filled with loud jolts and skin-tearing gore. British director Rob Savage has bragged that his film features 50 jump scares, that’s about one every two minutes, a boast that also indicates his exhausting priorities.

What’s strange is how unjumpy the film then is and how more interesting it feels when Savage isn’t trying to spill our popcorn. The Other Mommy is a double of working mother Ursula (Jessica Chastain), who has become a secret friend of young daughter Bela (Arabella Olivia Clark). She’s a demon who wants to become human and by impersonating Bela’s mother, she hopes that faking a deep connection will allow her “into her heart”. In a rather rushed fashion, Other Mommy’s campaign goes from teaser to full-court press.

Chastain is an actor who isn’t always a great fit, her admirable avoidance of being typecast leading to a too-wide variety of roles that just don’t always feel well suited. But her elegant iciness works wonders here, selling both a hard-working parent who struggles to soften at home and an untrustworthy monster trying to find the right emotional mode and facial expressions to convince a child that she isn’t nefarious. Both mommies are desperate to win her over and Chastain works hard to win us over in the process even if her overpronounced smile, used as the poster’s main image, is a little too reminiscent of the Smile series.

The rules of Other Mommy can also get a little scrambled. In trying to make Bela believe she is the gentle, loving and understanding parent she really needs, I’m not quite sure why she would keep presenting in such ghoulish and monstrous ways other than to scare those of us watching. The little blips are effective – the wrong amount of fingers, an accidental skin slip on her face – but too soon we have full-on gloopy body horror. The film can often feel like a loosely connected series of set pieces rather than a complete and cohesive story, something Chastain has experienced before in the It movies, which felt more like overlong trailers.

Savage managed to make one of the only genuinely necessary Covid movies with the ingenious Zoom horror Host , but his studio outings have so far lacked the same creative spark. Technically he proves himself once again here – as he did in the slickly made yet generic Stephen King adaptation The Boogeyman – but he’s in danger of becoming a studio horror director for hire rather than one with his own clear voice. There’s a slight sense of confused panic to his choices as he throws a little too much at the wall, Other Mommy’s abilities and guises so varied that she starts to lose any real distinctiveness as a villain, turning into just some industry standard monster to be mechanically expelled. It’s even more of problem when the set-up of the film itself is already so familiar (even in the last decade, it recalls Imaginary , M3gan , Z and Come Play ) and, as is often the case with so many horror films in this moment, a lot less would do so much more.

It’s also unclear how the two worlds are separated and operate, and while it’s refreshing to see characters all on the same page early on (both parents see Other Mommy within the first 20ish minutes), it’s then a struggle for the Succession screenwriter Nathan Elston to convincingly choreograph what comes next. Wouldn’t dad be a little more horrified earlier? Wouldn’t the police come calling after a gnarly midpoint death? Wouldn’t they not risk letting their daughter out of their sight? It’s amusingly grounded for a while (do we Google priests or mediums?) and there’s a neat and funny twist on what’s otherwise a rote Insidious-aping sequence, but the smarter ideas are mostly picked up briefly then dropped in favour of more basic funhouse horror. The psychological chaos inflicted by Other Mommy – pitting Bela against her parents, doing her bidding to try to impress her, forcing her to decide between the love she wants and the love she needs – is far scarier than yet more snappy but repetitive VFX. This wrestle is most apparent in the finale, which goes full house-rattling Poltergeist hokum and lightens the novel’s bleaker ending.

There’s a chillier, quieter version of Other Mommy that could have really crept under our skin, but Savage is too busy trying to give us a heart attack to care if he gives us nightmares.

Other Mommy is out in cinemas now

Jessica Chastain

Mas será que estamos diante de uma nova tendência criativa ou apenas de mais uma estratégia para aumentar as bilheterias? Essas versões realmente acrescentam algo à experiência cinematográfica ou servem apenas para convencer os fãs a pagarem novamente por um conteúdo que já consumiram? Existe alguma justificativa além do dinheiro?

article_text:
T he indie indulgences of US film-maker Amanda Kramer – which often contain big names making small appearances – are such a puzzle; sometimes they work, sometimes they don’t. I enjoyed her weird reverie about an imaginary 80s TV special, called Give Me Pity! , but not so much the 1950s-camp daydream Please Baby Please , with Andrea Riseborough. Now she gives us a film with a toweringly strange and potentially hilarious premise, on which the result does not in any way deliver. Yet there are moments of interest in the dreamy Lynchian drift that causes Kramer’s films to float away from the audience.

By Design is an all but unbearable absurdist drama. The actors deliver halting dialogue as if in a hypnotic trance, paralysed by the film’s heavy conceit: Juliette Lewis plays a depressed single woman who turns into a chair. The scene seems set for some entertaining hijinks with visual effects, in which Lewis and the chair merge. But no – not really. What in fact happens is that Lewis’s own body is supposedly robbed of its animating identity or spirit, which migrates into the chair while she becomes catatonic, a body flopped down on the bed. The chair itself doesn’t look or behave in any way differently.

Mamoudou Athie, doing his considerable best, plays a musician whose girlfriend buys him this haunted chair as a kind of guilt offering for walking out on him, and he becomes obsessed with it – although the comic or erotic potential of this transgressive idea is entirely neglected. The chair’s designer (a gamey cameo for the now late Udo Kier ) declares there is something strange about it but he can’t decide what it is. And so the film sleepwalks its way to a conclusion as unsatisfying as everything that has gone before. Someone somewhere should give Lewis a decent role.

article_text:
I n the early 1960s, when Peter Zumthor was a teenage apprentice in his father’s cabinet-making workshop, he designed his first cupboard. He later recalled the satisfaction of fitting the door so perfectly that it closed “with a special sucking sound”, saying his father instilled in him “the Basel pride in the well-built object” .

Six decades on, with a fleet of globally celebrated projects to his name, the 83-year-old Swiss architect is back in Basel, beaming with the same local pride. He is gazing out at his latest well-built object, which is also his first project here: a monolithic new gallery that looks chiselled from the earth, its layers of pale crumbly concrete hammered into shape, its big oak and bronze doors – their handles wrapped with leather cord – closing with that same satisfyingly expensive Swiss swoosh.

“It was an old feeling,” Zumthor tells me, describing working in his home town to build the £110m addition to the Beyeler Foundation . “I encountered craftspeople who remembered my father, who had this special knowledge of how to make things. They weren’t surprised if something had to be custom-made.”

It was quite a change from his previous building site. Fresh from the recent opening of the tortuous, two-decade-long, $724m addition to the Los Angeles County Museum of Art , Zumthor is visibly relieved to be back on home turf. “The normal American architect is used to sourcing products, not looking for somebody who can make something custom-made,” he says, with a furrowed brow. “Their buildings are an assembly of products.”

Not so in Switzerland . From the pear wood handrails to the leather benches and blown glass lamps, every piece of his new gallery has been meticulously handmade. But is the sum of these bespoke parts a worthy companion to one of the country’s – if not the world’s – most beloved art museums?

Designed by Italian architect Renzo Piano, the Beyeler Foundation was hailed as a model of elegant restraint when it opened in October 1997 – the same month as Frank Gehry’s billowing Bilbao Guggenheim – praised as a sober foil to the “iconic” tendencies of the time. Sited in Riehen, just outside Basel, in the grounds of an 18th-century villa, the museum was commissioned by Ernst Beyeler, Europe’s pre-eminent modern art dealer and co-founder of Art Basel, and his wife Hildy, to house their staggering collection of Monets and Mirós, Matisses and Picassos.

A long, low, temple-like shed nestled in a garden, the foundation contains within its porphyry walls a luminous sequence of galleries, with daylight flooding through slender rooftop louvers. Piano took his hi-tech fetish and wrapped it in a luxurious stone skin, foreshadowing his bigger museums to come. But it was too small right from the day it opened. Two years later, it was extended by 12 metres and soon became the most visited art museum in the country, receiving 500,000 visitors a year. The challenge was how to extend a museum already deemed perfect by its art world patrons.

“They wanted something completely different,” says Zumthor, who was selected from a shortlist of 11 architects in 2016, after 100 were approached for their ideas. “Renzo’s building is more industrial, whereas mine is almost domestic. It is the villa that this garden was missing.”

The foundation acquired the Iselin-Weber park, a formerly private woodland adjacent to the museum campus, which now doubles its size, and where Zumthor’s gallery rises like a rocky outcrop. It is one of three new structures he has designed, along with a five-storey, timber-clad office and art-handling block, and an auditorium pavilion, conceived as an open public lounge – a particularly appealing space that can be accessed without a ticket. “Ninety per cent of the time,” says the foundation’s director, Sam Keller, “museum auditoriums are dead spaces. So we’ve turned it into a social space for people to come and hang out, read books, listen to podcasts or do some work, a real extension of the park.”

The three buildings stand as an eclectic ensemble on either side of a lane, framing a public square of sorts, where a new drinking fountain trickles into a big stone trough, as in a traditional mountain village, welcoming art pilgrims to Zumthor-ville. Stone benches built into the museum facade greet weary wanderers. “A building is something you ought to be able to lean against every now and then,” says the architect, as Maurizio Cattelan’s unnerving sculpture of a drummer boy perches perilously on the parapet overhead, intermittently hammering his drum from the rooftop.

The chance for Zumthor to finally build in Basel, a few kilometres from his birthplace, clearly brought back fond memories. In a schmaltzy new two-hour documentary by Wim Wenders called From Inside Out, the misty-eyed architect explains that this “intimate building” has “a lot to do with me growing up here”. He recounts that Jura limestone was “the stone of my youth”, describing how the village fountains and the cattle troughs “all glowed”. He wanted his own building to glow, too, so he mixed Jura stone into the concrete, and had workers tamp the dry mixture by hand, laying it at a rate of no more than 45cm a day. This is all filmed with a stirring musical backdrop. He wanted the wobbly joints between each day’s work left visible, like strata of sedimentary rock.

“I call it ‘farmer concrete’,” he says. “You see it everywhere in the mountains. They make it themselves, and they don’t vibrate the mixture, so it looks rough like this. You can see the building has a history, that hands have worked on it. It’s nice if you can see those traces. If it’s too slick, you just look like a fashion magazine.”

Zumthor’s rugged brand of “rammed concrete” has become one of his highly published trademarks (and has indeed featured in fashion magazines ). There is a sense of him bringing his greatest hits to the Beyeler ensemble. He used the technique for the Bruder Klaus field chapel in rural Germany and a holiday house in Devon for Alain de Botton’s Living Architecture company. The admin block, meanwhile, bears a distinct resemblance to his atelier building in Haldenstein , also in Switzerland, its elegant oak facade (masking a concrete frame) crowned with a slender corrugated canopy.

And the pavilion draws on yet another language. It’s like a warm wooden womb that’s been dug into the landscape, surrounded by walls of glass and topped with a low upholstered acoustic ceiling, full of armchairs encouraging visitors to lounge awhile. Zumthor had to wait so long for a commission in his home town, he has turned one project into three.

The galleries themselves are quite a departure from Piano’s top-lit white cubes. After the gleaming stone exterior, the interior feels almost cave-like, Monet’s waterlilies looking muddier than ever in the ground-floor gloom. Things get brighter upstairs, with large picture windows framing pastoral views in different directions as you ascend the three floors, looking towards the Black Forest on one side and the Jura mountains on the other. Limestone terrazzo floors, lime-washed walls and pale concrete ceilings create an all-encompassing world of beige, which somehow flattens the work on show, relieved only by dark timber-lined nooks for loos and lifts.

Lozenge-shaped glass lamps (“made by the only two men in Italy who have the lung capacity to do it”, I am told) provide some ambient light, while spots highlight particular works. But you might find yourself pining for the celestial top-light of Piano’s galleries next door. Despite the architect’s protestations, it oozes the aura of a luxury boutique. As one visiting Angelino noted: “It feels like a new Skims store .”

The creamy promenade culminates in a roof terrace, with more views of pretty Swiss countryside, before visitors are shuttled down a pharaonic external stairway between the concrete walls, punched with triangular openings on one side, giving glimpses of the park and a mature ginkgo tree, around which the arms of the Y-shaped building extend. Questioned about the need for all this concrete, and its attendant carbon footprint, Zumthor is adamant. “I could not make a wooden museum,” he says. “I think it is not good for art. This kind of classical art needs more substance.”

He might have questioned his own assumptions. When it first opened, the Beyeler was praised for its brave departure from the fashions of the time. Thirty years on, Zumthor, for all his talk of sensitivity to place, has created something that feels as globally ubiquitous as the Louise Bourgeois spider that crouches in the garden outside. Like the menagerie of buildings by noted architects at the Vitra campus nearby, the foundation has succeeded in adding another familiar collectible to its haul of prized works.

article_text:
The Gotham Film & Media Institute will recognize Focus Features’ “ Elsinore ” with a Gotham Legacy Tribute at the Gotham Film Awards on Nov. 30, honoring the film’s subject, actor Ian Charleson.

The tribute, which takes place at Cipriani Wall Street in New York, will honor the film and its star Andrew Scott , screenwriter Stephen Beresford and director Simon Stone for bringing the legacy of actor and advocate Charleson to new audiences. Charleson, who died in 1990, was the star of the Oscar-winning “Chariots of Fire.”

“In his final months, Ian Charleson affirmed his talent, his determination, and what it means to be an actor,” said Jeffrey Sharp, Executive Director of The Gotham Film & Media Institute. “With Elsinore, Andrew Scott, Stephen Beresford, Simon Stone, and the entire production team have made a deeply moving film about a life devoted to performance and the community that supported him. We are delighted to celebrate Elsinore with the Gotham Legacy Tribute in recognition of the remarkable artist who inspired it.”

“Elsinore” tells the story of the Scottish actor who received a devastating AIDS diagnosis at the same time as has the chance to take on the stage role of a lifetime in “Hamlet.”

“’Elsinore’ follows an actor at the height of his powers as he strives to command the stage, facing his own mortality with unflinching honesty, wit, and grace. His final performance becomes his greatest triumph, and a source of healing and inspiration for those around him,” the synopsis reads.

In addition to Scott, “Elsinore” stars Olivia Colman, Billie Piper, Johnny Flynn, and Joe Locke. Colman plays Dr. Margaret Johnson, who treated Charleson and fellow gay men during the HIV epidemic, launching the first-ever dedicated HIV clinic.

“Elsinore” premiered at the Telluride Film Festival and went on to screen in the Special Presentations section at the Toronto International Film Festival, where it received the International People’s Choice Award.

It opens Nov. 20 in limited release and will expand over the Thanksgiving holiday and through December. “Elsinore” is produced by Studiocanal, LD Entertainment, Lucky Red and Magnolia Mae Films.

Also at the Gotham Awards , “Michael” will receive the musical tribute, “La Bola Negra” will receive the Vanguard Tribute, Danny Boyle will receive the director tribute for “Ink” and Laika will receive the anniversary tribute.

Nominees for the 36th annual Gotham Film Awards will be announced on Oct. 27.

article_text:
The leadership teams across divisions at the new Skydance are continuing to be hashed out, three weeks after the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger closed.

On Friday, Skydance chief communications officer Melissa Zukerman announced the senior members of her team in a memo to staff — and announced the departures of several execs.

In her memo, Zuckerman said Skydance has the opportunity to “rethink how we communicate – moving beyond traditional channels and finding new ways to reach people directly.” To that end, the company is launching a “direct to market” function focused on “expanding executive storytelling across our owned-and-operated platforms and identifying new channels and formats.”

That, according to Zuckerman, “will give us more ways to tell our own story, in our own voice, directly to the people we want to reach.”

Zuckerman’s four top lieutenants are: Laura Watson, EVP, head of corporate, executive and strategic communications (who joined Paramount in mid-2025 after leaving WBD); Shannon Buck, EVP, corporate communications and media relations (previously head of communications for Paramount+); Virginia Fout, EVP, global and executive events (previously owner/president of V Productions); and Deborah Marcus, SVP, head of corporate social responsibility (who joined Paramount in August 2025).

Zuckerman also thanked the comms teams members from Paramount and Warner Bros. who will be leaving the company: Arielle Falkowitz (WBD, SVP corporate relations and global events), Megan Klein (WBD, SVP communications), Joe Libonati (WBD, SVP communications), Adrienne O’Hara (WBD, EVP, chief communications and public affairs officer), Karen Shosfy (Paramount, SVP communications), Heather Wagoner (WBD, SVP internal communications, creative & brand) and Dennis Williams (WBD, SVP corporate social responsibility and corporate affairs).

Going forward, Zuckerman said she plans to hire “dedicated leaders” for financial communications and product and technology communications, “strengthening our capabilities in areas that will only become more important to our business — from AI tools for filmmakers and creatives to advertising sales and beyond.”

Read Zuckerman’s memo:

Team,

Communications is an essential part of how this company operates every day. Our role is to protect and promote our business and our people – advancing our priorities, strengthening our reputation and ensuring that those who matter to our success understand who we are, what we stand for and where we are going. To do that well, we need to be deeply connected to the business, close to our leaders and teams, and always ready to engage.

And we have an extraordinary opportunity in front of us. Few companies have the breadth of businesses, brands, content and creative talent that we do – or the ability to reach so many people in so many ways. We have a chance to harness the full power of that ecosystem, bringing greater creativity and impact to our communications and using our platforms to build stronger, more direct and meaningful connections.

David and Ynon have set three priorities: establish Skydance as the premier Hollywood content engine and home for the world’s leading storytellers; accelerate our integrated direct-to-consumer platform with great content, leading-edge technology and a superior fan experience; and optimize our highly profitable linear television portfolio, anchored by CBS. Underpinning all three is an ambition to build the most technologically capable media company – delivering more and better experiences for consumers, empowering our teams and operating with greater effectiveness, all while keeping human creativity at the heart of great storytelling.

Our job in Communications is to help move that strategy forward – by telling the stories of our storytellers, creatives, technologists and business leaders: their triumphs, their progress and, yes, their challenges. We build understanding of where we’re going and confidence in our ability to get there, making sure our words are always backed by our actions. We show, not tell – letting our work and our results speak for themselves, communicating with transparency and grounding everything we say in facts. That’s how we earn credibility and trust.

And we need an organization ready to deliver on that mandate. At its center is a Corporate Communications function responsible for enterprise and executive communications, working hand-in-hand with teams embedded across our businesses. It’s a model that has been tested and proven at Paramount – keeping us close to the business, coordinated across the company and operating in a no-surprises environment.

But structure is only part of the equation. We also have an opportunity to rethink how we communicate – moving beyond traditional channels and finding new ways to reach people directly. That ’s why we are launching a Direct to Market function focused on expanding executive storytelling across our owned-and-operated platforms and identifying new channels and formats. It will give us more ways to tell our own story, in our own voice, directly to the people we want to reach.

Of course, none of that lessens the importance of traditional communications and publicity – or of the press. Most of you know how strongly I believe in building and honoring relationships with journalists. Those relationships matter, and they are built on the same principles I expect us to bring to all our work: be direct, know your stuff and tell it like it is. Be accessible and responsive. And above all, earn trust by being credible, candid and grounded in the facts.

In a world of information overload, we know that communications extend far beyond what we say. It’s also about what we do and how we show up. That’s why I’m incredibly proud that our team also includes Corporate Social Responsibility, a group dedicated to extending our mission beyond our walls and using our platform to support the people, causes and communities where we can make a meaningful difference. By connecting our philanthropic partnerships with our content and broader storytelling, we have an opportunity not just to give back, but to strengthen the communities where we live and work.

Events are also a central part of our team and another powerful way we bring our story to life. Creating purposeful, memorable moments that celebrate our projects, champion our people and bring our communities together is an important part of how we build connection and showcase the incredible work happening across Skydance.

Delivering on all of this requires a team of thinkers and doers – people who can see what’s possible and then make it happen. Building that team for the future also requires difficult choices about how we organize, where we focus and how we work. I recognize that some of those choices mean saying goodbye to valued colleagues and changing ways of working that have been familiar for a long time. But our success depends on our willingness to evolve and build differently for what’s ahead. I’m incredibly proud of the team we are putting in place, starting with my immediate leadership team, who will help drive this work forward: Laura Watson, Shannon Buck, Virginia Fout and Deborah Marcus.

Laura Watson, EVP, Head of Corporate, Executive and Strategic Communications. Many of you know Laura as my deputy and a key partner across every part of our business. She oversees our strategic and internal communications, enterprise messaging and executive communications and speechwriting.

Shannon Buck, EVP, Corporate Communications and Media Relations. Shannon joins us from her most recent role leading communications for Paramount+. She will work closely with our businesses to identify, shape and elevate our most important stories – including across DTC, advertising, marketing and distribution – and help bring together the right platforms, talent and voices to tell them.

Virginia Fout, EVP, Global and Executive Events. Virginia leads our global events, hospitality and executive hosting, bringing our company and our story to life through the experiences we create. She will play an integral role in ensuring that our voice, priorities and brand are reflected consistently across our most important events and engagements.

Deborah Marcus, SVP, Head of CSR. Deb has transformed CSR from a traditional giving function into a powerful platform for storytelling, engagement and social impact. Most recently, she launched the ‘Ebenezer No Kid Hungry ’ campaign and is now building our companywide Season of Giving, creating meaningful ways for our people and brands to make a difference in the communities we serve.

We are building this organization to operate as one team, with close partnerships across every part of the business. In that spirit, Chris Ender, Brooke Robertson and Jeff Cusson, Comms Leads for Skydance TV, Studios and DTC, respectively, dotted line into my leadership team, helping ensure we stay connected, coordinated and aligned in service of the company’s priorities. We also collaborate with other businesses, including Games & Experiences, Consumer Products, Government Relations, News and Sports, to ensure the same level of connection and support across the company.

I feel incredibly fortunate to have this A-list team in place – and we’re not done yet. As we build for what’s ahead, we will add dedicated leaders in Financial Communications and Product and Technology Communications, strengthening our capabilities in areas that will only become more important to our business – from AI tools for filmmakers and creatives to advertising sales and beyond.

I also want to extend a special thanks to the Comms colleagues who will be leaving the organization: Arielle Falkowitz, Megan Klein, Joe Libonati, Adrienne O’Hara, Karen Shosfy, Heather Wagoner and Dennis Williams. We are grateful for their partnership and many contributions. Please join me in thanking them and wishing them the very best.

We have an incredible opportunity ahead of us, and I’m excited about what we can accomplish together. Thank you for everything you bring to this team every day.

Melissa

article_text:
Clayface might have been a considerably nicher choice for a feature film than DC’s “Supergirl” and “Superman,” but that didn’t stop audiences from showing out to catch the Batman supervillain’s gory, nightmare-inducing origin story at the box office this weekend.

The new release generated $10.4 million from 3,458 North American theaters on Friday, taking the No. 1 spot. It’s a strong start for the film, which looks to pull in $24 million by Sunday.

Related Stories

Directed by James Watkins, “Clayface” follows the titular Batman villain, a rising movie star also known as Matt Hagen (Tom Rhys Harries), who volunteers for a highly experimental medical procedure after his face is severely disfigured. Naomi Ackie, David Dencik, Max Minghella and Eddie Marsan also star. Variety’s Guy Lodge called the film “its own ugly animal; perhaps the characters and conflicts introduced here would pall if given the franchise treatment, but in the context of a single, genre-melding romp, they’re fresh and ickily enjoyable.”

Popular on Variety

Fellow DC films like “Superman,” produced for nearly $230 million, brought in $618.72 million worldwide over the course of its 2025 theatrical run, while “Supergirl” was considered a bomb with $126 million against a $170 million budget earlier this year. In comparison, “Clayface” cost $44 million to produce.

A24’s much-hyped Elizabeth Holmes documentary “ You Can See Everything ” landed in second place on Friday, making $6.14 million from 2,655 North American theaters, up from 855 at opening weekend. The buzzy doc has made $31.7 million domestically so far. Rival estimates suggest the film will gross another $20 million by Sunday.

Comedian Nathan Fielder and “Primetime” filmmaker Lance Oppenheim quietly worked on the movie for more than three years, which offers an unhinged look at the Theranos founder a month before she began an 11-year prison sentence for defrauding investors. In addition to being eligible for best documentary feature at the 99th Academy Awards, the film will also be submitted across the board as seen on A24’s awards site: best picture, director, production design, cinematography, costume design, film editing, makeup and hairstyling, sound and original score.

Laika’s “ Wildwood ,” another new release, landed in third place on Friday, grossing $4.28 million from 2,942 North American theaters. Featuring a voice cast that includes Carey Mulligan, Jacob Tremblay and others, the stop-motion film looks to bring in $11.2 million by Sunday.

Directed by Travis Knight, “Wildwood” revolves around a teenage girl who travels with a classmate into an enchanted forest after her brother is abducted. Strong reviews should continue to propel the lavish film at the box office, which carries a substantial $100 million price tag.

Black Bear’s “ Wicker ” followed in fourth place, earning $2.36 million on Friday from 1,471 North American theaters. The offbeat romantic comedy, directed by Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston Fischer, is targeting a $5.5 million opening weekend.

Described as an “audacious comedic fable,” “Wicker” tells the love story of an ostracized fisherwoman (Olivia Colman) who commissions a husband from the local basketmaker (Peter Dinklage). Alexander Skarsgård plays said husband. Elizabeth Debicki also stars.

Coming in fifth was Legendary Entertainment’s “Street Fighter.” The action film grossed $2.34 million on Friday and should add another $8.4 million by Sunday, bringing its cumulative gross to $46.7 million.

“Street Fighter,” directed by Kitao Sakurai, stars Noah Centineo and Andrew Koji as two estranged fighters in the 90s who are recruited to enter a tournament that forces them to face off against each other.

article_text:
「アルベール・マルケ展」がSOMPO美術館（東京・新宿）で12月13日まで開催されています。フランス近代絵画の巨匠であり、親友のアンリ・マティスと共に「フォーヴィスム（野獣派）」の誕生に関わった画家アルベール・マルケ（1875～1947年）の、日本では35年ぶりの回顧展です。

本展ではマルケが生涯をかけて好み、表現し続けた「水辺の景色」に注目。グッズ売り場でも、マルケが描き出した水辺の情景を旅する気分を味えるアイテムが充実していました。

ステッカー 990円

「水辺の景色」の前に、まず紹介したいのがこちらのステッカー。マルケの素描「幸福な男」がモチーフとなっています。 水面や空に吸い込まれそうになるマルケ作品ですが、近づいて見ると、ほんのわずかな線で人や船などをいきいきと表していることに驚かされました。その不思議な魅力と卓越したデッサン力を手元で堪能できるステッカーです。

さて、ここからは「幸福な男」がグッズにまつわる土地をご案内します。

ファイル 550円

マルケが繰り返し描いた、パリのノートル＝ダム大聖堂とセーヌ河岸を背に、散策を楽しむ「幸福な男」。

街の空気や匂いが立ち込めてくるようです。独自の「灰色」やニュアンスに富んだ中間色など、マルケならではの色彩の魅力も存分に味わえるクリアファイルです。

ポーチ 2,750円

「マルセイユの馬」に描かれている、歴史ある港町マルセイユ。行き交う人々や馬で賑わっています。

作品から飛び出してきたような、馬のチャームがかわいい！

馬のご挨拶にびっくり！

一筆箋 770円

マルケの故郷のフランス・ボルドーにも近い保養地ル・ピラです。

みずみずしく透き通るような水面は、幸福感に満ちあふれています。「幸福な男」もうっとり。

PETブックマーカー 495円

「ラ・グレットの窓」がデザインされています。透明度の高いPET製のしおりで、チュニジアの港町ラ・グレットに思いを馳せましょう。

以上、5点で計5,555円でした。

（読売新聞美術展ナビ編集班・美間実沙 撮影・吉成）
